description: We’re a team of four with backgrounds in AI, physics, and data engineering, passionate about using technology and scientific thinking to solve real-world challenges. Our skills include Python, machine learning, LLMs, and data analytics. We’re looking for teammates with skills in geospatial analysis, NASA Earth data, web development, or UI/UX design. If you enjoy creative problem-solving, collaboration, and building sustainable, impactful solutions, join us!
summary:
We built Terrestrial Analog Explorer, a live web map that identifies the places on Earth that best match specific Moon and Mars sites, including permanent Moon base and landing locations. 
It scores 32 Earth sites against 7 targets, among them the lunar south pole, a lunar lava-tube pit, Jezero Crater and Arcadia Planitia. 
Each score combines NASA POWER climate data with geology, and each target is characterized with LRO LOLA and MGS MOLA terrain.
The method is validated: it ranks established analogs such as the Dry Valleys, Death Valley and Haughton Crater in the top 6 for every target. That lets us trust its new findings. 
Saudi Arabia's Umm Jirsan lava tube is the best cave analog for both the Moon and Mars, and Egypt's Kamil Crater best matches lunar mare plains. 
At the lunar south pole, a landing-site finder locates flat, sunlit patches within about 2 km of likely ice.
This matters because analog sites are often chosen by tradition. Our tool makes the choice measurable and transparent, and surfaces under-used sites for testing equipment before missions fly.
details:
What it does
EcoSignals Analog Explorer is a live web map that identifies the places on Earth that best match specific Moon and Mars sites. Users pick a target: the lunar south pole (Artemis base region), the Mare Tranquillitatis lava-tube pit, Hadley Rille, or on Mars Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, Arcadia Planitia or the Arsia Mons cave skylights. All 32 Earth candidates are re-scored instantly on a NASA Blue Marble map. A slider shifts the weight between climate and geology. Clicking a site opens a side-by-side comparison with the target and a link to NASA Worldview. Each target also shows its own terrain from mission data, and lunar sites link to LROC QuickMap imagery.

How it works

  1. Characterize each target: temperature, daily temperature swing, water, vegetation and nine geology features. Terrain comes from LRO LOLA (Moon) and MGS MOLA (Mars).
  2. Score each Earth site from 0 to 100: 50% climate similarity using NASA POWER 2001–2025 data, 50% geology match. Moon and Mars extremes are clamped to the most extreme values Earth reaches.
  3. Validate: the method must rank known analogs (Dry Valleys, Death Valley, Lanzarote, Haughton Crater) in the top 6 for all 7 targets. It does, which lets us trust its new findings.
  4. Find landing sites: around the lunar south pole, every 240 m cell is scored on sunlight, slope (under 8°) and distance to permanent shadow, where ice is likely.

Key findings

  • Umm Jirsan lava tube (Saudi Arabia) is the best cave analog for both the Moon (72.4) and Mars (72.0), ahead of Lanzarote (65.2) and Kilauea (61.8). It is not yet used as an analog.
  • Kamil Crater (Egypt) is the top match for lunar mare plains and #2 for Jezero Crater.
  • Arcadia Planitia has only 37 m of local relief and a 0.05° slope, ideal for a base. The Arsia cave skylights offer shelter but sit at +10 km, with about 246 Pa of air.
  • The exact lunar south pole is a poor landing site: only 4.8% of the area is flat enough, with 19% sunlight. Our finder locates 6 better patches 41–69 km away, with 19–38% sunlight, each within 2.1 km of permanent shadow.

Benefits and impact
Analog site selection becomes measurable, transparent and repeatable, with every number traceable to NASA data. Mission and research teams can justify site choices per target and discover under-used analogs, many in under-studied regions of the Middle East, North Africa and Central Asia.

Creativity
Instead of listing "Mars-like places", we score Earth against specific targets and validate the method on known analogs before trusting new results. We also go beyond Earth: the lunar landing-site finder combines slope, sunlight and ice proximity, the same trade-offs Artemis planners face.

Factors we considered
The coarse 50 km NASA POWER grid misrepresents small or high-altitude sites, so five sites are flagged in the app. Geology uses simple yes/no features from the literature. Earth cannot match lunar extremes, so we compare against the closest values Earth reaches. Next steps: 1 km MODIS data, partner-agency radar roughness (CSA, ESA) and spectral geology.

Tools
Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, Pillow), React, Vite and Leaflet, hosted on Vercel. Code: https://github.com/vidyashreerayar/NASA_EcoSignals
